extracted.intended_audience: writers and editors (journalists, encyclopaedists, Wikipedia editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing the opening paragraph (the 'lead' or 'lede') for articles, book chapters, and other written works, covering journalistic, encyclopedic, and magazine styles. Describes purpose, typical content (e.g., 5Ws+H for news), anti-patterns (burying the lead), and variation by genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic leads should grab attention
rubrics_metrics.description: "Journalistic leads emphasize grabbing the attention of the reader."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic leads are intended to engage readers immediately; they prioritize the most interesting or attention-grabbing elements of a story. Failure to do so (see 'burying the lead') reduces immediate reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: News leads should answer the basic questions (who, what, why, when, where, how)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Most standard news leads include brief answers to the questions of who, what, why, when, where, and how the key event in the story took place."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong news lead succinctly supplies the essential facts of the event. In newspaper writing this first paragraph that summarizes or introduces the story is also called the 'blurb paragraph', 'teaser text' or (UK) the 'standfirst'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid burying the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: "In journalism, the failure to mention the most important, interesting or attention-grabbing elements of a story in the first paragraph is sometimes called 'burying the lead'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burying the lead can be used deliberately to tease readers or to conceal politically inconvenient or embarrassing information, but as an anti-pattern it means readers won't see the most important facts up front. Avoid delaying the key facts unless there is a clear, intentional editorial reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encyclopaedia leads should define the subject and emphasize interesting points
rubrics_metrics.description: "Encyclopaedia leads tend to define the subject matter as well as emphasize the interesting points of the article."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For reference works the lead's primary purpose is definition and summary of scope, with a secondary goal of highlighting notable or interesting aspects. This contrasts with the priority on attention-grabbing and immediate event facts in journalistic leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match lead style and length to genre and intent
rubrics_metrics.description: "Leads vary enormously in length, intent, and content depending on the genre of the piece."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature and general magazine articles may sit between journalistic and encyclopaedic styles and often lack a distinct lead paragraph entirely. Choose lead length, tone, and content consistent with genre expectations and the piece's communicative goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductory lines/standfirsts exist as distinct summary elements
rubrics_metrics.description: "In journalism, there is the concept of an introductory or summary line or brief paragraph, located immediately above or below the headline, and typographically distinct from the body of the article. This can be referred to with a variety of terms, including: the standfirst (UK), kicker (US), bank head(line), deck, dek, or subhead (US)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used, these typographically distinct summary lines serve to introduce or summarize the story separately from the lead paragraph; consider whether a standfirst/deck is appropriate for the publication's conventions and whether it complements or replaces the opening paragraph.
